data.title: Initial Level Placement
data.description: A high-level scan to establish your current CEFR baseline (A2-B2). One question per grammar point across three bands.

sections.explain: 'Will' is followed by the base verb, with no '-s' and no 'to': 'will rain'. Modal 'will' never takes 'to' or a third-person '-s'.

words.word: I think it will rain tomorrow.
I think it will rains tomorrow.
I think it will to rain tomorrow.

sections.explain: 'Should' gives advice and is followed by the base verb: 'should see'. It never takes 'to' or an '-ing' form.

words.word: You should seeing a doctor.
You should to see a doctor.
You should see a doctor.

sections.explain: Possessive pronouns stand alone: 'mine', 'yours'. We don't use the adjective forms 'my/your' without a noun, and 'yours' has no apostrophe.

words.word: This book is mine, not yours.
This book is my, not your.
This book is mine, not your's.

sections.explain: Use the past perfect ('had' + past participle) for the earlier of two past actions: 'had left' happened before 'arrived'. 'has left' is present perfect, and 'had leave' lacks the participle 'left'.

words.word: The train has left before we arrived.
The train had leave before we arrived.
The train had left before we arrived.

sections.explain: Use 'who' for people in a defining relative clause: 'the man who lives...'. 'Which' is for things, and we don't repeat the subject ('who he lives').

words.word: The man who lives next door is a doctor.
The man which lives next door is a doctor.
The man who he lives next door is a doctor.

sections.explain: The past passive is 'was/were' + past participle: 'was built'. 'was build' uses the base verb, and 'is built' (present) doesn't fit the past date 1890.

words.word: The bridge was built in 1890.
The bridge is built in 1890.
The bridge was build in 1890.

sections.explain: In a subject question the question word is the subject, so use no auxiliary 'do/did': 'Who broke the window?'. 'Who did break/broke' incorrectly adds 'did'.

words.word: Who did break the window?
Who did broke the window?
Who broke the window?

sections.explain: 'Needn't have' + past participle means an action was done but was unnecessary: 'You needn't have brought a gift'. 'needn't had' and 'didn't need have' are not correct forms.

words.word: You didn't need have brought a gift.
You needn't have brought a gift.
You needn't had brought a gift.

sections.explain: Passive reporting uses 'is believed/said/thought' + 'to have' + past participle: 'is believed to have left'. 'to have leave' lacks the participle, and 'believes' reverses the meaning.

words.word: The suspect believes to have left the country.
The suspect is believed to have leave the country.
The suspect is believed to have left the country.

sections.explain: Non-defining relative clauses add extra information between commas and use 'who'/'which', not 'that': 'My brother, who lives in Paris, ...'. 'that' is not used in non-defining clauses, and the commas are required.

words.word: My brother who lives in Paris is visiting us.
My brother, that lives in Paris, is visiting us.
My brother, who lives in Paris, is visiting us.
